title: How is heap memory divided (Young Generation with Eden/Survivor, Old Generation, Metaspace)?

s1_definition.profdef: The heap is split by generation to match how long objects live. The Young Generation holds newly created objects and is subdivided into Eden, where objects are first allocated, and two Survivor spaces, S0 and S1, used to copy surviving objects during minor collections. Objects that survive enough minor collections are promoted to the Old Generation, which holds long-lived objects. Metaspace is separate from the heap and lives in native memory, holding class metadata rather than objects. This generational layout lets the collector run cheap, frequent minor collections on the young area and rarer, expensive collections on the old area.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India sorting paperwork by how long it will be needed. Brand-new transaction slips land in the busy intake tray, which is Eden. Most slips are dealt with and thrown away within minutes, so the cleanup crew sweeps Eden often and quickly. The few slips that are still needed get moved to a holding tray, the Survivor space, and if a slip keeps surviving these sweeps it clearly matters for the long term, so it is filed in the permanent archive room, the Old Generation. The rulebook of form types is kept in a totally separate room, Metaspace, because it is not paperwork at all but the templates themselves.
s1_definition.oneliner: The heap is Young (Eden plus two Survivor spaces) for short-lived objects and Old for long-lived ones, with Metaspace outside the heap in native memory for class metadata.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The heap is split by generation to match how long objects live. The Young Generation holds newly created objects and is subdivided into Eden, where objects are first allocated, and two Survivor spaces, S0 and S1, used to copy surviving objects during minor collections. Objects that survive enough minor collections are promoted to the Old Generation, which holds long-lived objects. Metaspace is separate from the heap and lives in native memory, holding class metadata rather than objects. This generational layout lets the collector run cheap, frequent minor collections on the young area and rarer, expensive collections on the old area.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India sorting paperwork by how long it will be needed. Brand-new transaction slips land in the busy intake tray, which is Eden. Most slips are dealt with and thrown away within minutes, so the cleanup crew sweeps Eden often and quickly. The few slips that are still needed get moved to a holding tray, the Survivor space, and if a slip keeps surviving these sweeps it clearly matters for the long term, so it is filed in the permanent archive room, the Old Generation. The rulebook of form types is kept in a totally separate room, Metaspace, because it is not paperwork at all but the templates themselves.

**One line to remember:** The heap is Young (Eden plus two Survivor spaces) for short-lived objects and Old for long-lived ones, with Metaspace outside the heap in native memory for class metadata.

sections.s2_technical:
The generational design rests on a well-known observation called the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. A banking request creates lots of temporary objects, like DTOs and intermediate BigDecimals, that are discarded almost immediately. Splitting the heap lets the collector focus cheap effort where most garbage is.

The Young Generation is where new objects are allocated, and it has three parts. Eden is the main allocation area; `new Account(...)` typically lands in Eden. The two Survivor spaces, S0 and S1, are used during a minor garbage collection. When Eden fills up, a minor collection copies the still-reachable objects from Eden and the in-use Survivor space into the other Survivor space, and then wipes Eden and the now-empty Survivor clean. One Survivor space is always empty between collections by design.

Each object carries an age counter that increases every time it survives a minor collection. When an object's age crosses the tenuring threshold, which defaults to fifteen, it is promoted to the Old Generation, also called the Tenured Generation. The Old Generation holds objects that have proven they live long, such as a long-lived cache or a connection pool. Collecting the old area is more expensive, so it happens far less often, and a collection that includes the old area is what people loosely call a major or full collection.

Metaspace is not part of the heap at all. Since Java 8 it lives in native memory and stores class metadata, method information, and the runtime constant pool, growing as classes are loaded and bounded by `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`. It replaced the fixed PermGen. A senior nuance is that modern collectors like G1 organize the heap into many equal-sized regions rather than fixed contiguous blocks, and dynamically label regions as Eden, Survivor, or Old, but the generational concept still applies. Another nuance is that very large objects may be allocated directly in the Old Generation to avoid pointless copying. You can observe all of this with `-Xlog:gc*` or a tool like VisualVM.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's statement generator creates millions of tiny temporary objects while formatting each line of a statement, and almost all of them are discarded instantly. The team worried this would slow the system with constant garbage collection. This is exactly why the Young Generation exists, because those short-lived formatting objects are born in Eden and swept away by cheap, fast minor collections before they ever reach the expensive Old Generation.

Problem 2 — The same service keeps a long-lived in-memory cache of frequently accessed accounts like Rajesh's and Priya's, which must survive for hours. This is exactly what the Old Generation is for, because objects that keep surviving minor collections are promoted to the old area where collection is rare, so the cache is not disturbed on every sweep.

In the mini-project we simulate this. We define an `Account`, a `StatementGenerator` that creates many short-lived line objects, and an `AccountCache` that holds long-lived accounts. The demo generates statement lines for Rajesh and Priya, producing lots of young garbage, while keeping the cache alive, and logs how many temporary objects were created versus how many cached objects persist. We run it with GC logging so the reader can connect the code to young versus old behavior.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/heap/HeapDemo.java

# Run with GC logging to observe Young vs Old collections
java -Xms64m -Xmx128m -Xlog:gc*:stdout:time,level,tags \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.heap.HeapDemo

# Watch for many cheap "Pause Young" events; cached accounts stay promoted.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two long-lived accounts, Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), placed in a cache, and 100000 short-lived statement lines generated per account.

Step 1: The cache is created and Rajesh and Priya are put into it. Their Account objects start life in Eden like everything else, but because the cache keeps strong references to them, they will survive collections and eventually be promoted.

Step 2: The generator starts creating StatementLine objects, one per loop iteration. Each new StatementLine is allocated in Eden. As the loop runs, Eden fills quickly because hundreds of thousands of tiny objects are being created.

Step 3: When Eden fills, a minor garbage collection runs. It finds that almost every StatementLine is already unreachable, because each one is replaced on the next loop iteration, so it reclaims them cheaply. The still-referenced cached accounts are copied to a Survivor space, and their age counters increase.

Step 4: As the loop keeps running and more minor collections occur, the cached Rajesh and Priya accounts keep surviving. Once their age crosses the tenuring threshold, they are promoted from the Young Generation to the Old Generation, where collections are rare, so they are no longer disturbed on every sweep.

Step 5: After the loop, the demo logs how many short-lived objects were created, which is a very large number of young garbage, and confirms the cached accounts are still alive and reachable. Metaspace, meanwhile, simply held the class metadata for Account, StatementLine, and the rest, unaffected by all this object churn.

```text
[INFO] Short-lived StatementLine objects created (young gen): 200000
[INFO] Long-lived cached accounts (old gen candidates): 2
[INFO] Cached Rajesh still alive: Rajesh
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  new StatementLine(...)            new Account(...) put in cache
        │ allocate                        │ allocate
        ▼                                 ▼
  ┌──────────────── YOUNG GENERATION ─────────────────┐
  │  Eden  ──minor GC──▶ Survivor S0 ⇄ S1  (age++)     │
  │  (most StatementLines die here, swept cheaply)     │
  └───────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                          │ age ≥ tenuring threshold (15)
                          ▼
  ┌──────────────── OLD GENERATION ───────────────────┐
  │  cached Rajesh, Priya (long-lived)                 │
  │  collected rarely (major/full GC)                  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────── METASPACE (native, NOT heap) ──────────────┐
  │  class metadata: Account, StatementLine, ...        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Heap Sizing for a Statement Service ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Statement Service JVM (per pod)                      │
  │  HEAP (-Xmx 128m)                                     │
  │   ├─ Young Gen (Eden + S0 + S1)  ← high churn         │
  │   │    sized larger for short-lived statement lines   │
  │   └─ Old Gen                     ← account cache      │
  │  METASPACE (native, MaxMetaspaceSize) ← class meta    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Tuning: bigger Young Gen → fewer promotions → fewer full GCs.
  Monitored via Prometheus JVM metrics + GC logs → Grafana.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Object placement and promotion ═══

  ── Allocation rules ──
  small new object        → Eden
  survives 1 minor GC     → Survivor (age 1)
  survives N minor GCs    → age N; age ≥ 15 → promote to Old
  very large object       → may go straight to Old (skip copy)

  ── Collection cost ──
  Minor GC (Young only)   → frequent, cheap, copying collection
  Major/Full GC (Old)     → rare, expensive, stop-the-world

  ── Where things are ──
  StatementLine (temp)    → Eden → quickly unreachable → reclaimed
  Account (cached)        → Eden → Survivor → Old (long-lived)
  class metadata          → Metaspace (native, not heap)

  Observe with: -Xlog:gc*  or VisualVM / Java Flight Recorder
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The heap is divided by generation because of a simple empirical truth the JVM relies on, which is that most objects die young. In banking code a single request creates many temporary objects like DTOs and intermediate BigDecimals that are discarded almost immediately, so splitting the heap lets the garbage collector concentrate cheap, frequent effort exactly where most of the garbage is.

The Young Generation is where new objects are allocated, and it has three parts. Eden is the main allocation space, so a freshly created object normally lands there. The two Survivor spaces, S0 and S1, are used during a minor collection: when Eden fills up, the collector copies the still-reachable objects from Eden and the active Survivor into the other Survivor, then wipes the rest clean, and by design one Survivor space is always empty between collections. Each surviving object carries an age counter that increases on every minor collection it lives through.

When an object's age crosses the tenuring threshold, which defaults to fifteen, it is promoted to the Old Generation, which holds objects that have proven they live a long time, like a connection pool or an in-memory cache. Collecting the Old Generation is far more expensive, so it happens much less often, and a collection that touches the old area is what people loosely call a major or full collection. Metaspace is separate from the heap entirely; since Java 8 it lives in native memory and holds class metadata and the runtime constant pool rather than objects, and it replaced the old fixed-size PermGen.

In my banking work this maps directly to behavior I have tuned. A statement generator creates millions of short-lived line objects that are born in Eden and swept away cheaply before they ever reach the Old Generation, while a long-lived account cache survives repeated minor collections and gets promoted to the Old Generation where it is left alone. One senior nuance I always add is that modern collectors like G1 split the heap into many equal-sized regions and label them as Eden, Survivor, or Old dynamically rather than using fixed contiguous blocks, and that very large objects may be allocated straight into the Old Generation to avoid wasteful copying. So my complete answer is that the heap is split into a Young Generation made of Eden plus two Survivor spaces for short-lived objects and an Old Generation for long-lived ones, promotion is driven by surviving enough minor collections, and Metaspace sits outside the heap in native memory for class metadata.

---

keyPoints: Young Generation: newly created objects — Eden + Survivor spaces (S0, S1)
Old Generation (Tenured): long-lived objects promoted from Young
Eden: where new objects are allocated first
Survivors: objects that survive Minor GC move here (S0 and S1 swap each cycle)
Metaspace (Java 8+): class metadata — replaced PermGen, uses native memory
